amend-easy-forgot.label: Add a forgotten file to the last commit

You committed login.py as "Add auth module", then noticed logout.py is still sitting in your folder. Half an auth module isn't a module, and you haven't shared the commit with anyone.

amend-easy-forgot.task: Include src/logout.py in the latest local commit while keeping its message Add auth module. Finish on main.

Going through your history, Maeve points at a commit that says only "Update text". It reworded the login screen, but nobody reading the log would guess that. The files are right. You haven't pushed it.

amend-easy-login-copy-message.task: Change the latest local commit message to Clarify login copy. Keep its files as they are and finish on main.

Starting point: You are on main; local branches include main.
amend-easy-navbar-message.task: Change the latest local commit message to Adjust navbar spacing. Keep its files as they are and finish on main.

amend-easy-readme-message.task: Change the latest local commit message to Clarify setup requirements. Keep its files as they are and finish on main.

Starting point: You are on main; local branches include main.
amend-easy-typo.task: Change the latest local commit message to Initial commit. Keep its files as they are and finish on main.

amend-hard-auth-message-and-test.task: Include tests/test_auth.py in the latest local commit and change its message to Add auth validation coverage. Finish on main.

amend-hard-convention.task: Change the latest local commit message to Update Terraform staging environment configuration. Keep its files as they are and finish on main.

amend-medium-export-doc.task: Include docs/export.md in the latest local commit while keeping its message Document export flow update. Finish on main.

bc-easy-capstone-db.task: Create feature/database-models from the current tip of main and switch to it. Finish on feature/database-models.

You are already on main at its latest commit, the version the team uses as the starting point for urgent repairs. “Keep this one focused,” he says. Give the incident a branch named hotfix/session-timeout and switch to it so the repair can be reviewed on its own.

Starting point: You are on main; available local branches: main.
bc-easy-corp-hotfix.task: Create hotfix/session-timeout from the current tip of main and switch to it. Finish on hotfix/session-timeout.

bc-hard-review-snap.real_world_context: A temporary review branch can mark an older snapshot. You can then return to main without losing the convenient name for that commit.
bc-hard-review-snap.story:
You checked out an old version to review how a release behaved, and the review is taking longer than expected. Sage says, “Give this snapshot a name so we can find it again tomorrow.” Your terminal is at that older commit with no active branch. Create review/v1-snapshot at the position you are viewing, then go back to main for your regular work. The review branch should remain as a pointer to the snapshot.

Starting point: You are at a commit without an active branch; available local branches: main.
bc-hard-review-snap.task: Create review/v1-snapshot at the detached commit you are viewing, then return to main. Keep the review branch.

bc-med-oss-develop.label: Create feature/docs-update from develop's tip
bc-med-oss-develop.real_world_context: Open source projects sometimes use develop for new contributions. A branch made while on develop starts from that line’s current commit.
bc-med-oss-develop.story:
You have cloned an open source project and found its contribution guide. New work begins from develop, even though a main branch also exists. Raven points to the documentation ticket and says, “A small guide update is a good first contribution.” You are already on develop, so its latest commit is the correct base. Create feature/docs-update here and switch to it; starting from main would miss the development work the maintainers expect.

bc-med-oss-develop.task: Create feature/docs-update from the current tip of develop and switch to it. Finish on feature/docs-update.

be6.label: Rebase feature/recovery onto main
be6.real_world_context: Rebase replays a branch’s commits on a new base, giving a linear feature history. The commit IDs change, so verify the result.
be6.story:
Finn is preparing a code freeze when he notices your feature/recovery branch split from main several commits ago. The team has since added changes to main, and your feature commits still sit on the older base. “Put your work on top of what we have now,” he says. You are on feature/recovery. Rebase it onto current main, then inspect the graph to confirm the feature follows the updated base and the working folder is clean.

Starting point: You are on feature/recovery; available local branches: main, feature/recovery.
be6.task: Rebase the current feature branch onto main, then inspect the complete commit graph to verify the order. Finish with clean working files.

be7.label: Rebase feature/search-filters onto main
be7.real_world_context: Building filters on the updated main gives reviewers a branch based on the latest application shell.
be7.story:
You have been building search filters while another teammate refreshed the application shell on main. Finn wants the filter branch to begin from that newer foundation before review. You are on feature/search-filters, which has diverged from main. “Replay your commits after the shell update so the reviewer sees a clean line,” he says. Rebase onto main, then inspect the commit graph to verify the new order and leave no unfinished changes.

Starting point: You are on feature/search-filters; available local branches: main, feature/search-filters.
be7.task: Rebase the current feature branch onto main, then inspect the complete commit graph to verify the order. Finish with clean working files.

be8.label: Rebase feature/cli-flags onto main
be8.real_world_context: A rebased feature can include newer fixes from main beneath its own commits; the graph helps confirm their order.
be8.story:
The command-line tool gained two fixes on main while you were adding optional flags in feature/cli-flags. Finn opens the history and sees parallel lines. “The flags should sit on top of those fixes,” he says, pointing at the updated main branch. You are already on feature/cli-flags. Rebase your branch onto main and inspect the graph afterward so the team can confirm the rewritten feature history is linear and complete.

Starting point: You are on feature/cli-flags; available local branches: main, feature/cli-flags.
be8.task: Rebase the current feature branch onto main, then inspect the complete commit graph to verify the order. Finish with clean working files.

bh6.label: Recover the dropped commit on feature/cli-flags
bh6.real_world_context: A faulty rebase can omit a commit. The reflog may reveal the original tip; finding it and restoring it before rebasing preserves the complete feature.
bh6.story:
Sage reviews feature/cli-flags after a teammate’s rebase and cannot find the commit that adds the silent-mode flag. The flag was committed before, so the original position should still appear in Git’s recent reflog. You are on the feature branch. “I want the whole feature on today’s main, with nothing missing,” she says.

Starting point: You are on feature/cli-flags; available local branches: main, feature/cli-flags.
bh6.task: Bring the complete feature back, including the commit that went missing, and place the whole branch on top of current main. Finish with clean working files.

bh7.label: Recover the dropped commit on hotfix/export-csv
bh7.real_world_context: Recovering the pre-rebase hotfix tip restores the test commit, then replays the whole branch onto the newer base.
bh7.story:
The CSV export hotfix has been rebased onto main, but Raven notices that its test commit disappeared. The original branch tip is still recoverable in the reflog. You are on hotfix/export-csv, and candidate c5 contains the complete pre-rebase work. “Let’s get the tests back before we call this ready,” Raven says. The finished hotfix must sit on current main with its tests included.

Starting point: You are on hotfix/export-csv; available local branches: main, hotfix/export-csv.
bh7.task: Bring back the complete hotfix, including its missing test commit, and place the whole branch on top of current main. Finish with clean working files.

bh8.label: Finish a rebase after fixing a conflict
bh8.real_world_context: While a rebase is paused, Git replays your commits one at a time and stops when one of them conflicts. The conflict must be resolved, and the rebase told to carry on, before the branch is whole again. Git marks the disputed lines with <<<<<<<, =======, and >>>>>>> lines; the finished file must contain none of them.
bh8.story:
Sage rebased feature/rate-limits onto main so the team could review a straight history, but Git stopped on a conflict in src/limiter.py. Main added a limit name, and the feature added a retry count, so both belong in the result. The rebase is still paused and the branch looks half-built. “Finish the rebase properly,” Sage says. “Don’t leave the branch in this state overnight.”

Starting point: You are in the middle of a rebase of feature/rate-limits onto main, stopped on a conflict in src/limiter.py; available local branches: main, feature/rate-limits.
bh8.task: Resolve src/limiter.py so it contains exactly the lines shown below, with no conflict markers, and finish the rebase. The finished branch must sit on top of main with all its commits.

bm6.label: Move fix/footer-typo onto main
bm6.real_world_context: Replaying onto a new base can move only commits after an accidental parent branch onto main, keeping the unwanted redesign out.
bm6.story:
Sage asks for a typo correction in the site footer. You finish it, then notice you started fix/footer-typo from the unapproved feature/checkout-redesign branch instead of main. “We can ship the spelling fix without bringing in the redesign,” Sage says. You are on the typo branch. Inspect the branch graph, then replay only the typo branch’s own commits onto main, leaving the checkout redesign behind. Finish on the corrected fix branch.

Starting point: You are on fix/footer-typo; available local branches: main, feature/checkout-redesign, fix/footer-typo.
bm6.task: Inspect the graph, then replay only the commits unique to fix/footer-typo after feature/checkout-redesign onto main. Finish on fix/footer-typo with clean working files.

The hotfix itself is wanted, but the beta commits are not. You are on the hotfix branch. “Let’s move just your repair onto main,” Finn says. Inspect the graph to identify the old base, then replay only the hotfix commits onto current main and keep the beta work out.

Starting point: You are on hotfix/login-timeout; available local branches: main, release/2.0-beta, hotfix/login-timeout.
bm7.task: Inspect the graph, then replay only the commits unique to hotfix/login-timeout after release/2.0-beta onto main. Finish on hotfix/login-timeout with clean working files.

Finn starts rebasing feature/export-pdf onto main so it can ship this week, but Git stops halfway on a conflict in src/export.py. The two versions of that file differ in ways nobody on the team understands yet, and Finn would rather have a calm conversation than guess. “Put the branch back the way it was,” he says. “We'll sort the rebase out tomorrow.” You are in the middle of the unfinished rebase.

Starting point: You are in the middle of a rebase of feature/export-pdf onto main, stopped on a conflict in src/export.py; available local branches: main, feature/export-pdf.
bm8.task: Cancel the unfinished rebase so feature/export-pdf is exactly as it was before the rebase started.

You changed how the profile card behaves when a borrower has no photo, and src/profile-card.js is ready. In the same folder, notes/profile-ideas.md holds your running thoughts: a few good ideas, a few bad ones, and a reminder to change the logo color. Sage is about to pull the group's latest work.

commit-hard-profile-distractor.task: Stage src/profile-card.js and create a commit with the message Update profile card behavior. Leave notes/profile-ideas.md uncommitted; finish on main.

commit-hard-search-two-targets-one-distr.label: Commit search ranking display, leave notes out
commit-hard-search-two-targets-one-distr.real_world_context: The search handler and template make one visible update; planning notes remain unfinished. Staging the two product files keeps the commit complete and focused.
commit-hard-search-two-targets-one-distr.story:
You changed how search results are ranked, which touched both src/search.js and templates/search.html, and neither works without the other. While planning the next step you also started notes/search-ranking.md, a rough outline that isn't ready for anyone. Raven plans to build the demo version tonight from whatever has been saved.

Starting point: You are on main; local branches include main; working files include src/search.js, templates/search.html, notes/search-ranking.md.
commit-hard-search-two-targets-one-distr.task: Stage src/search.js, templates/search.html and create a commit with the message Refine search ranking display. Leave notes/search-ranking.md uncommitted; finish on main.

commit-hard-selective.label: Commit handler fix, leave experimental file out
commit-hard-selective.real_world_context: A ready handler fix can be reviewed while an experimental file stays local. Choosing only the finished file keeps the commit focused on the null-check bug.
commit-hard-selective.story:
A librarian added a book with no title and the whole request crashed. The cause was a missing null check in api/handler.py, and you fixed it this afternoon. You are also halfway through a faster lookup in api/experimental.py, which sometimes works and sometimes returns nothing. Raven is demoing to the department tomorrow, and the experiment is not something anyone should show.

Starting point: You are on main; local branches include main; working files include api/handler.py, api/experimental.py.
commit-hard-selective.task: Stage api/handler.py and create a commit with the message Fix request handler null check. Leave api/experimental.py uncommitted; finish on main.

commit-med-docker.label: Commit Docker configuration
commit-med-docker.real_world_context: Container setup depends on both the build instructions and example environment settings. Saving them together keeps the configuration change coherent.
commit-med-docker.story:
Half the group can't run the project because their setups differ. Raven asks you to package it so every laptop behaves the same. You wrote a Dockerfile and a matching .env.example listing the settings each teammate must fill in. One without the other leaves a teammate with a setup that half works.

Starting point: You are on main; local branches include main; working files include Dockerfile, .env.example.
commit-med-docker.task: Stage Dockerfile, .env.example and create a commit with the message Add Docker configuration. Finish on main.

commit-medium-export-flow.label: Commit export flow update
commit-medium-export-flow.real_world_context: When export behavior changes, its instructions should match. Saving the code and documentation together avoids a history point where they disagree.
commit-medium-export-flow.story:
Maeve asked how a librarian would export the borrowing report, and you realized the real answer had changed since anyone wrote it down. You updated src/export.py and rewrote docs/export.md to match. Code and documentation that disagree are worse than no documentation.

Starting point: You are on main; local branches include main; working files include src/export.py, docs/export.md.
commit-medium-export-flow.task: Stage src/export.py, docs/export.md and create a commit with the message Document export flow update. Finish on main.

commit-medium-profile-card.label: Commit profile card layout
commit-medium-profile-card.real_world_context: The profile card’s behavior and styling change together. A commit containing both files presents one complete layout update for review.
commit-medium-profile-card.story:
You redesigned the borrower profile card. The new layout needs both the JavaScript that builds the card and the stylesheet that arranges it, and either one alone would render a broken card. Finn will review the redesign as a single piece of work tomorrow morning.

Starting point: You are on main; local branches include main; working files include src/profile-card.js, styles/profile-card.css.
commit-medium-profile-card.task: Stage src/profile-card.js, styles/profile-card.css and create a commit with the message Update profile card layout. Finish on main.

commit-medium-search-results.label: Commit search results view
commit-medium-search-results.real_world_context: A search view can involve both the handler and the page template. Committing the pair together captures the behavior the user actually sees.
commit-medium-search-results.story:
Catalog search used to return a plain list of titles. Your version shows author and availability, which meant changing the handler in src/search.js and the layout in templates/search.html. Sage is testing the borrowing flow tomorrow and needs search to work as a whole, not half rewritten.

Starting point: You are on main; local branches include main; working files include src/search.js, templates/search.html.
commit-medium-search-results.task: Stage src/search.js, templates/search.html and create a commit with the message Refine search results view. Finish on main.

e1.label: Recover an accidental reset
e1.real_world_context: A hard reset moves a branch pointer and can discard working edits, but a recent committed tip may still be reachable through the reflog. A new branch can preserve it.
e1.story:
A hard reset has moved main backward, and the commits you finished earlier no longer appear at its tip. Raven sees the alarm on your face and says, “Git may still remember where we were.” The repository’s recent reflog contains a candidate at c3. You are on main, which should remain where the reset left it for now.

Starting point: You are on main; available local branches: main.
e1.task: Recover the commit that was main’s tip before the reset onto a new branch named recovery/e1, and switch to it. Leave main where the reset left it.

e2.label: Recover after a script reset
e2.real_world_context: An automated reset can hide commits from ordinary branch history. Checking the reflog and commit contents helps recover the correct point.
e2.story:
A teammate’s cleanup script runs a hard reset on your project branch. Sage notices that the latest completed commits have disappeared from the visible main history. “Let’s look for the position from before the script ran,” she says. You are on main, with no recovery branch yet. The recent reflog leads to candidate c3; check what it contains. Once you confirm it, create recovery/e2 at that commit and move onto the recovered branch.

Starting point: You are on main; available local branches: main.
e2.task: Recover the commit that was main’s tip before the reset onto a new branch named recovery/e2, and switch to it. Leave main where the reset left it.

e3.label: Recover after resetting too far
e3.real_world_context: Recovering on a new branch preserves the former tip while leaving the reset main in place for comparison.
e3.story:
You meant to remove one bad commit but reset farther back than planned. Finn compares the current main with your notes and sees that several good commits have gone missing too. “Don’t guess at a reset target twice,” he says. You are still on main. Use Git’s reflog to locate the former tip at c3, inspect that commit, and create recovery/e3 there. The new branch preserves the lost position without moving main again.

Starting point: You are on main; available local branches: main.
e3.task: Recover the commit that was main’s tip before the reset onto a new branch named recovery/e3, and switch to it. Leave main where the reset left it.

e4.label: Recover after a merge reset
e4.real_world_context: The reflog records recent movements of HEAD and branches. Inspecting a candidate commit before naming it avoids preserving the wrong position.
e4.story:
A merge attempt leaves the team confused, and you run a hard reset to get a clean working folder. Finn checks the history and realizes the reset went past several useful commits. “We can recover a pointer before we decide what to merge next,” he says. You are on main. Find the lost tip in recent reflog, inspect candidate c3, then create and switch to recovery/e4 at that commit.

Starting point: You are on main; available local branches: main.
e4.task: Recover the commit that was main’s tip before the reset onto a new branch named recovery/e4, and switch to it. Leave main where the reset left it.

e5.label: Recover a debugging reset
e5.real_world_context: Committed work is often still reachable shortly after a mistaken reset. A recovery branch gives it a stable name.
e5.story:
While debugging a failing test, you run a hard reset and later realize you needed the commits that were at the old tip. Finn asks you to stop making new edits until you have a safe copy of that point. You are on main; the candidate in the reflog is c3. Then create recovery/e5 at the lost tip and switch to it, leaving the reset main untouched.

Starting point: You are on main; available local branches: main.
e5.task: Recover the commit that was main’s tip before the reset onto a new branch named recovery/e5, and switch to it. Leave main where the reset left it.

fetch-easy-cap-check.label: Fetch to update origin/feature/models tracking
fetch-easy-cap-check.real_world_context: Fetching lets the group inspect the model classes on origin/feature/models without immediately changing local feature work.
fetch-easy-cap-check.story:
Your capstone groupmate announces in chat, “I pushed the model classes.” You are on local feature/models, where your own edits may still need review. Raven suggests looking at the remote branch before deciding whether to bring in the teammate’s commits. The shared repository is origin. Fetch its latest information so origin/feature/models is current, but do not move your local feature branch in this step.

Starting point: You are on feature/models; available local branches: feature/models; origin is available.
fetch-easy-cap-check.task: Update your remote tracking information from origin so you can see the latest origin/feature/models. Do not integrate it into your local branch yet.

fetch-easy-corp-list.label: Fetch to update origin/release/v2 tracking
fetch-easy-corp-list.real_world_context: An updated release branch on the server appears in your remote tracking information after a fetch; your local release branch is not moved by that step.
fetch-easy-corp-list.story:
Sage tells the team that the release engineer has updated release/v2 on the server. You are on the local release branch and want to see that remote state before changing your checkout. The project uses origin as its remote. “First just refresh our view of the server,” Sage says. Fetch so the remote tracking information is current; do not integrate the release commits into local release/v2 yet.

fetch-easy-corp-list.task: Update your remote tracking information from origin so you can see the latest origin/release/v2. Do not integrate it into your local branch yet.

fetch-hard-oss-review.label: Review incoming work on release/next, then update it
fetch-hard-oss-review.real_world_context: After a large upstream change, reviewing is a separate act from integrating; only the second one changes your local release/next.
fetch-hard-oss-review.story:
A maintainer has just merged a large contribution into remote release/next. Raven asks you to review what changed before folding it into your own release branch. You are on local release/next, and origin is configured.

fetch-hard-oss-review.task: A teammate has pushed new commits to release/next. Look at exactly what is new on origin before it joins your branch, then make your local release/next include it.

h1.label: Recover an accidental reset
h1.real_world_context: Busy reflogs may contain several movements. Verify the selected commit instead of assuming the first entry is the right one.
h1.story:
After a hard reset, main no longer shows the work you finished this morning, and the ordinary log can't bring it back. Sage points out that the reflog records every place main has been, including positions the log has forgotten. Sage wants the right commit identified and checked before anything gets a name.

Starting point: You are on main; available local branches: main. The reflog includes candidate commits c3 and c4 after repeated checkouts and resets. Commit c3 contains the borrower search fix; c4 contains an abandoned search experiment. No old position has a branch name. The working tree is clean.
h1.task: Find the lost work among the old positions in the reflog. Recover the commit containing the borrower search fix on a new branch named recovery/h1, then switch to that branch. Reject the candidate containing an abandoned search experiment. Leave main at its reset position and keep the working tree clean.

h2.label: Recover after a script reset
h2.real_world_context: Recent scripts and manual commands can create confusing movement records. Recover a confirmed commit with a new branch.
h2.story:
A cleanup script reset main while Finn was collecting changes for review. The reflog now has several entries close together, and it would be easy to pick the wrong one. "We need the most recent lost tip, not just any old commit," Finn says. main is not to move again during the recovery.

Starting point: You are on main; available local branches: main. The reflog includes candidate commits c3 and c4 after repeated checkouts and resets. Commit c3 contains the completed borrowing report; c4 contains an earlier draft of the report. No old position has a branch name. The working tree is clean.
h2.task: Find the lost work among the old positions in the reflog. Recover the commit containing the completed borrowing report on a new branch named recovery/h2, then switch to that branch. Reject the candidate containing an earlier draft of the report. Leave main at its reset position and keep the working tree clean.

h3.label: Recover after resetting too far
h3.real_world_context: When several earlier positions are visible, inspecting c3 helps distinguish the desired former tip from an unrelated movement.
h3.story:
Maeve spots a surprising gap in main after you reset farther back than you meant to. The reflog shows enough activity that a quick glance could be misleading. She asks you to check the candidates before relying on any of them.

Starting point: You are on main; available local branches: main. The reflog includes candidate commits c3 and c4 after repeated checkouts and resets. Commit c3 contains the validation fix and its passing test; c4 contains a cleanup that does not include the validation fix. No old position has a branch name. The working tree is clean.
h3.task: Find the lost work among the old positions in the reflog. Recover the commit containing the validation fix and its passing test on a new branch named recovery/h3, then switch to that branch. Reject the candidate containing a cleanup that does not include the validation fix. Leave main at its reset position and keep the working tree clean.

h4.label: Recover after a merge reset
h4.real_world_context: A merge and reset can create multiple reflog entries. A new pointer at the verified former tip preserves the committed work.
h4.story:
Sage's merge attempt went wrong, so the group backed out with a hard reset, and then discovered the reset had hidden good work too. Several movements happened during the attempt, so choosing the first entry you see would be careless. "Check the candidate before you restore anything," Sage says.

Starting point: You are on main; available local branches: main. The reflog includes candidate commits c3 and c4 after repeated checkouts and resets. Commit c3 contains the working export before the failed merge; c4 contains the failed merge result. No old position has a branch name. The working tree is clean.
h4.task: Find the lost work among the old positions in the reflog. Recover the commit containing the working export before the failed merge on a new branch named recovery/h4, then switch to that branch. Reject the candidate containing the failed merge result. Leave main at its reset position and keep the working tree clean.

h5.label: Recover a debugging reset
h5.real_world_context: Even a late reset need not require rebuilding committed changes by hand if the former tip remains reachable in the reflog.
h5.story:
A late debugging session ends with a hard reset, followed by the uncomfortable discovery that the previous tip of main has vanished from its visible history. Raven helps you read through the recent reflog entries. "Let's confirm what's in the commit before we save a branch at it," she says.

Starting point: You are on main; available local branches: main. The reflog includes candidate commits c3 and c4 after repeated checkouts and resets. Commit c3 contains the final login timeout fix; c4 contains a temporary debugging change. No old position has a branch name. The working tree is clean.
h5.task: Find the lost work among the old positions in the reflog. Recover the commit containing the final login timeout fix on a new branch named recovery/h5, then switch to that branch. Reject the candidate containing a temporary debugging change. Leave main at its reset position and keep the working tree clean.

init-easy-current-empty.label: Initialize the current folder
init-easy-current-empty.real_world_context: Teams often begin with an ordinary folder. Initializing it gives Git a place to record future snapshots, while the files remain unstaged until someone deliberately adds them.
init-easy-current-empty.story:
Your team has finally started its first project together. Raven, your group leader, has created the project folder, assigned the work, and confidently announced that everyone should “stay organized.” Ten minutes later, someone asks whether they should make a backup before editing, and another teammate suggests copying the folder every afternoon. Raven pauses. “Let’s avoid creating a museum of backup folders.” Nothing has been recorded yet, and the current folder has no version control. Before anyone starts changing files, the team needs a way to keep track of its work. You have been given the setup job; the first actual snapshot will come later.

Starting point: You are in an empty project folder. It is not a repository yet.
init-easy-current-empty.task: Initialize the current directory as a Git repository with main as its initial branch. Do not stage files or create a commit.

init-easy-invoice.label: Initialize invoice-tracker
init-easy-invoice.real_world_context: A client project can grow beyond its first brief. Giving invoice-tracker its own repository prepares a change history the developer can use as new requests arrive.
init-easy-invoice.story:
Your first freelance client wants a simple invoice tracker: customer names, amounts, and payment status. Then the follow-up messages arrive. Could it also handle overdue invoices? Discounts? A printable receipt with a slightly bigger logo? Raven, your group leader, reads the conversation and smiles. “Congratulations. Your simple project has discovered its personality.” You haven’t written any code yet, and there is no project repository. Before those requests start turning into files, you need a dedicated workspace called invoice-tracker with version control ready. The client can keep thinking about the logo while you give the project a more dependable beginning.

Starting point: You are in your workspace. There is no invoice-tracker folder yet.
init-easy-invoice.task: Create a new invoice-tracker folder that is a Git repository, with main as its first branch.

init-easy-trunk-branch.label: Initialize with trunk as the first branch
init-easy-trunk-branch.real_world_context: Branch names appear in build scripts, review instructions, and teammate habits. Starting this repository on trunk avoids a naming mismatch before work begins.
init-easy-trunk-branch.story:
It’s your first morning at a software company, and Sage is helping you prepare your workspace. The onboarding guide looks straightforward until you notice that the team calls its main development line trunk. You ask whether that is a typo. “Nope. Someone picked the tree metaphor years ago, and now we’re committed,” Sage says, pointing to the same name in the build instructions and team handbook. Your current project folder is still outside version control. Before development begins, its setup needs to match the team’s naming convention. Sage promises the rest of onboarding involves fewer trees, although you haven’t reached the branching discussion yet.

Starting point: You are in an empty project folder. It is not a repository yet.
init-easy-trunk-branch.task: Initialize the current directory as a Git repository with trunk as its initial branch.

init-hard-ci.label: Initialize ci-configs
init-hard-ci.real_world_context: Pipeline configuration deserves a clear repository boundary. Initializing ci-configs alone avoids treating the surrounding deployment workspace as part of its history.
init-hard-ci.story:
The operations team has asked you to prepare ci-configs, a dedicated repository for pipeline configuration. Finn has already left a build file at pipelines/build.yml in the surrounding workspace, alongside material from other tasks. His handover message is impressively brief: “Please get the repository ready before the deployment meeting.” You look at the clock, then at the collection of folders. There is enough time to do this carefully, but not enough to untangle an oversized repository afterward. The requested project needs its own boundary, and the existing workspace files need to remain where they are while you prepare it.

Starting point: You are in a workspace that contains pipelines/build.yml and folders from other tasks. The folder ci-configs does not exist yet.
init-hard-ci.task: Create a repository in a new ci-configs folder, with main as its first branch. Leave every other file in the workspace where it is.

init-hard-research-log.label: Initialize research-log subfolder only
init-hard-research-log.real_world_context: A parent folder can hold several unrelated projects. Initializing only research-log keeps notes and archive outside its repository while preserving the existing files.
init-hard-research-log.story:
Finn’s workspace contains three very different kinds of material: current research in research-log, rough ideas in notes, and old work in archive. Unfortunately, they all sit beneath the same parent folder, making it easy to mistake the whole collection for one project. “The archive includes an approach we abandoned for excellent reasons,” Finn explains. “It doesn’t need a comeback.” Only research-log should receive its own version control, with main as the initial branch. The parent workspace and its neighboring folders must remain outside it. The existing files should come through the preparation untouched.

Starting point: You are in a parent folder that contains research-log, notes and archive. None of them is a repository.
init-hard-research-log.task: Initialize only the research-log subfolder as a Git repository with main as its initial branch. Leave the parent folder and the sibling folders outside the repository.

init-hard-safe-rerun.label: Safely reinitialize the current repository
init-hard-safe-rerun.real_world_context: Maintenance scripts sometimes repeat initialization. Running it inside an existing repository should keep the recorded commits, current branch, and uncommitted edits intact.
init-hard-safe-rerun.story:
Sage is reviewing a maintenance script when you notice that it repeats repository setup inside release-notes. The folder is already a repository: it has one commit, main is active, and notes/today.md contains work that hasn’t been committed yet. You point this out before running anything. “Good catch,” Sage says. “A maintenance script should leave us with fewer questions, not a missing afternoon.” The setup step still needs to be repeated as part of the check. This time, success means keeping what already exists: the same recorded history, the same branch position, and every current file edit intact.

Starting point: You are in release-notes. It is already a repository with one commit, you are on main, and notes/today.md has uncommitted edits.
init-hard-safe-rerun.task: Run repository initialization again in the current repository. Keep its existing commit, its main branch and every uncommitted change.

init-hard-ui-kit.label: Initialize ui-kit with trunk
init-hard-ui-kit.real_world_context: The design kit, brand artwork, and experiments have different owners and lifecycles. Setting up only ui-kit with trunk gives only the kit its own history and matches the team’s naming rule.
init-hard-ui-kit.story:
The design team is turning its reusable interface styles into a proper project. Inside the parent workspace, ui-kit contains the actual kit, brand-assets holds the company artwork, and experiments contains several ideas that seemed better during the meeting. Finn opens the last folder, considers a glowing navigation bar, and closes it again. “Let’s keep that discussion for another day.” Only ui-kit should become a repository. Its initial branch must be named trunk. The brand assets, experiments, and existing file contents all need to stay as they are.

Starting point: You are in a parent folder that contains ui-kit, brand-assets and experiments. None of them is a repository.
init-hard-ui-kit.task: Initialize only the ui-kit subfolder as a Git repository with trunk as its initial branch. Leave the parent and sibling folders untouched.

init-med-oss.label: Initialize oss-contrib
init-med-oss.real_world_context: Contribution notes and practice changes are easier to manage in their own workspace. An oss-contrib repository lets this preparation evolve without mixing it with unrelated local projects.
init-med-oss.story:
You have found an open-source project you’d love to contribute to, but opening its issue tracker feels like walking into a conversation that started three years ago. Finn, your teammate, suggests a smaller first step: prepare a local practice workspace where you can organize your contribution notes and try ideas before touching the real project. “You don’t have to fix the entire internet this afternoon,” he says. The workspace should be called oss-contrib, and it needs its own version control. There is no existing repository there yet. For now, your assignment is simply to give your preparation work a proper home.

Starting point: You are in your workspace. There is no oss-contrib folder yet.
init-med-oss.task: Create a new oss-contrib folder that is a Git repository, with main as its first branch.

init-medium-docs-site.label: Initialize docs-site
init-medium-docs-site.real_world_context: Documentation changes need a shared, reviewable history, especially when several teammates hold different copies. A separate docs-site repository gives those revisions one home.
init-medium-docs-site.story:
A new teammate has spent the morning following installation instructions scattered across a chat thread, an old presentation, and a document titled “Use This One.” By lunch, the team agrees that its documentation needs a proper home. Sage volunteers to organize the content, then discovers that three people have different copies of the setup guide. “Wonderful. We already have a research project,” she says. The team decides to keep its new documentation site in a separate workspace called docs-site. Before Sage starts gathering pages, you need to prepare that workspace with version control so future improvements can be tracked together.

Starting point: You are in your workspace. There is no docs-site folder yet.
init-medium-docs-site.task: Create a new docs-site folder that is a Git repository, with main as its first branch.

init-medium-quiet-research-log.label: Initialize field-notes with existing files
init-medium-quiet-research-log.real_world_context: Many projects begin as an ordinary folder. Starting a repository in an existing folder leaves its files exactly as they are and lets future changes be recorded.
init-medium-quiet-research-log.story:
A field researcher has kept weeks of observations in a folder called field-notes: a notes.txt file and a data.csv file. Sage looks at the folder, then at the file dates, and asks the question nobody wants to hear: “What happens if one of these gets overwritten?” Nothing has ever tracked these files, and neither has been touched today. Sage wants the folder under version control before the next field trip, but without changing a single file inside it. No renamed files, no first commit yet. The files simply need a history to start from.

Starting point: You are in your workspace. The folder field-notes already contains notes.txt and data.csv. It is not a repository yet.
init-medium-quiet-research-log.task: Make the existing field-notes folder a Git repository with main as its first branch. Do not stage or commit its files.

init-medium-trunk-api-playground.label: Initialize api-playground with trunk
init-medium-trunk-api-playground.real_world_context: Experiments can be isolated from production code while still being tracked. Starting api-playground on the team’s trunk convention makes even this sandbox follow their usual workflow.
init-medium-trunk-api-playground.story:
Raven wants somewhere to test API ideas without cluttering the team’s production project. Yesterday’s quick experiment produced six files, two promising approaches, and one endpoint nobody remembers writing. “Let’s give the experiments an actual address,” she says. The team has chosen api-playground as the new workspace name. It will be separate from the production code, but it still needs to follow the team’s convention of naming the initial branch trunk. No repository has been prepared there yet. Your job is to get the space ready before the next round of experiments spreads across someone’s desktop again.

Starting point: You are in your workspace. There is no api-playground folder yet.
init-medium-trunk-api-playground.task: Create a new api-playground folder that is a Git repository, with trunk as its first branch.

m1.label: Recover an accidental reset
m1.real_world_context: The visible log follows the current branch; the reflog can show positions that branch used to occupy.
m1.story:
Sage asks for a feature you committed yesterday, but it is missing from main after an accidental hard reset. You remember the work was committed, just not exactly which movement entry points to it. “Let’s trace the old tip rather than rebuilding it,” Sage says. You are on main.

Starting point: You are on main; available local branches: main.
m1.task: Recover the commit that was main’s tip before the reset onto a new branch named recovery/m1, and switch to it. Leave main where the reset left it.

m2.label: Recover after a script reset
m2.real_world_context: A clean working folder does not prove a reset kept every commit. Verify the old tip itself before creating a recovery branch.
m2.story:
Finn is reviewing the build when an automated script unexpectedly resets main. The working folder looks clean, which almost hides the fact that recent commits are no longer at the branch tip. “Clean isn’t the same as complete,” he says. You are on main.

Starting point: You are on main; available local branches: main.
m2.task: Recover the commit that was main’s tip before the reset onto a new branch named recovery/m2, and switch to it. Leave main where the reset left it.

m3.label: Recover after resetting too far
m3.real_world_context: An overly broad reset changes where main points. Naming the old commit recovers access without another reset.
m3.story:
You wanted to drop a single test commit and used a hard reset, but the branch moved past several other commits as well. Maeve notices the gap during review. “Before changing anything else, let’s keep a pointer to the old work,” she says. You are on main.

Starting point: You are on main; available local branches: main.
m3.task: Recover the commit that was main’s tip before the reset onto a new branch named recovery/m3, and switch to it. Leave main where the reset left it.

m4.label: Recover after a merge reset

Merging feature/checkout-copy into main stops in two files, src/checkout.js and src/receipt.js, and each needs its own decision. Sage opens the merge tool and says, “It takes the files one at a time. Don’t rush the second one.” You are on main.

Starting point: You are on main; available local branches: main, feature/checkout-copy; the next merge will report conflicts in two files.
mergetool-medium-router.task: Merge feature/checkout-copy into your current main branch. Use the simulator’s merge tool to resolve both files so that each contains exactly the lines shown below, with no conflict markers. Complete the merge with the default merge message.

partial-easy-auth-validation.label: Stage the auth validation hunk only
partial-easy-auth-validation.real_world_context: A narrow validation fix can be released before a larger auth refactor is finished. Partial staging separates the safe fix from the ongoing work.
partial-easy-auth-validation.story:
Halfway through a large cleanup of src/auth.py, you spotted a validation bug and fixed it. The cleanup is nowhere near done, but the bug fix can't wait. Raven hit it while testing the sign-in page.

Starting point: You are on main; local branches include main; working files include src/auth.py.
partial-easy-auth-validation.task: Stage only the auth validation fix and commit it with the message Fix auth validation. Leave The unfinished refactor out of the commit and finish on main.

partial-easy-billing.label: Stage the billing fix hunk only
partial-easy-billing.real_world_context: A rounding fix and temporary print statements can live in the same file. Partial staging saves the client-ready fix while the diagnostic experiment stays in the working copy.
partial-easy-billing.story:
You fixed a rounding error in src/billing.py, then added a few print statements further down the same file to see what the numbers looked like. Maeve is checking the project tonight, and the group needs the rounding fix saved now. The prints were only ever for you.

Starting point: You are on main; local branches include main; working files include src/billing.py.
partial-easy-billing.task: Stage only the billing rounding fix and commit it with the message Fix billing calculation rounding error. Leave The diagnostic print statements out of the commit and finish on main.

partial-easy-export-format.label: Stage the export formatting hunk only
partial-easy-export-format.real_world_context: The formatting fix can stand on its own while new logging remains experimental. Selecting just that hunk produces a focused export change.
partial-easy-export-format.story:
Librarians complained that exported dates came out in the wrong format. You fixed it in src/export.py and, to see what was happening, added some temporary logging lines in the same file. Finn wants the format fix in before the weekly build, and nobody wants the logging there.

Starting point: You are on main; local branches include main; working files include src/export.py.
partial-easy-export-format.task: Stage only the export formatting fix and commit it with the message Fix export formatting. Leave The extra logging out of the commit and finish on main.

partial-easy-routes.label: Stage the routes handler hunk only
partial-easy-routes.real_world_context: Updated route handlers are ready before the experimental middleware. Staging only the handler hunk prevents an unreviewed auth idea from joining the commit.
partial-easy-routes.story:
src/routes.py holds two pieces of work: the updated route handlers, which are finished, and an experimental auth middleware you commented out after starting it on a whim. Finn is waiting on the handlers to connect the frontend. Both changes sit in the same file, which makes this awkward.

Starting point: You are on main; local branches include main; working files include src/routes.py.
partial-easy-routes.task: Stage only the updated route handlers and commit it with the message Update API route handlers. Leave The experimental auth middleware out of the commit and finish on main.

partial-easy-search-ranking.label: Stage the search ranking hunk only
partial-easy-search-ranking.real_world_context: A ranking correction and code cleanup may have different review risks. Committing only the correction keeps its effect easy to assess.
partial-easy-search-ranking.story:
In src/search.py you corrected the ranking so exact title matches come first, and while you were there you started tidying the surrounding code. Sage is demoing search to Maeve tomorrow and needs the ranking fix. The tidying is unfinished.

Starting point: You are on main; local branches include main; working files include src/search.py.
partial-easy-search-ranking.task: Stage only the ranking algorithm fix and commit it with the message Fix search ranking. Leave The cleanup refactor out of the commit and finish on main.

partial-hard-auth-cross-file.label: Stage validation hunks across auth code and tests
partial-hard-auth-cross-file.real_world_context: A validation fix is meaningful alongside its matching test. Partial staging can take those two hunks across files without sweeping in the refactor, cleanup, or debug notes.
partial-hard-auth-cross-file.story:
Your validation fix touched two files, src/auth.py and tests/test_auth.py, and in each one there's also unfinished work: a refactor in the code and a cleanup in the tests. notes/auth-debug.md is still around from debugging. Maeve wants one commit that shows the fix and the test that proves it, and nothing else.

Starting point: You are on main; local branches include main; working files include src/auth.py, tests/test_auth.py, notes/auth-debug.md.
partial-hard-auth-cross-file.task: Stage only the auth validation fix and matching test and commit it with the message Fix auth validation and add its test. Leave The refactor, test cleanup, and debug notes out of the commit and finish on main.

partial-hard-export-cross-file.label: Stage formatting hunks across export code and tests
partial-hard-export-cross-file.real_world_context: The export formatting fix and its test form one change. Selecting their hunks keeps extra logging, test cleanup, and follow-up notes for later.
partial-hard-export-cross-file.story:
Fixing the export date format meant changing src/export.py and tests/test_export.py. Each file also has changes that don't belong to the fix: logging in the code and a cleanup in the tests. notes/export-followup.md is waiting beside them. Raven wants a commit that tells the story of the format fix and nothing else.

Starting point: You are on main; local branches include main; working files include src/export.py, tests/test_export.py, notes/export-followup.md.
partial-hard-export-cross-file.task: Stage only the export formatting fix and matching test and commit it with the message Fix export formatting and add its test. Leave The logging, test cleanup, and follow-up notes out of the commit and finish on main.

partial-hard-search-cross-file.label: Stage ranking hunks across search code and tests
partial-hard-search-cross-file.real_world_context: The ranking logic and its test should be reviewed together. The unrelated cleanup, fixture edits, and temporary output can remain outside this commit.
partial-hard-search-cross-file.story:
The ranking change touched src/search.py and tests/test_search.py, and each file also carries something unrelated: cleanup in the code, a fixture tidy-up in the tests. A tmp/search-output.txt file is lying around from a test run. Sage is going to cite this commit as the one that fixed ranking, so it should contain exactly that.

Starting point: You are on main; local branches include main; working files include src/search.py, tests/test_search.py, tmp/search-output.txt.
partial-hard-search-cross-file.task: Stage only the search ranking fix and matching test and commit it with the message Fix search ranking and add its test. Leave The cleanup, fixture edits, and temporary output out of the commit and finish on main.

partial-hard-terraform.label: Stage only the network Terraform hunk
partial-hard-terraform.real_world_context: Network configuration and experimental feature flags share a Terraform file. Saving only the network hunk keeps unapproved flags and debug material out of the infrastructure change.
partial-hard-terraform.story:
Your group deploys its project from terraform/main.tf. In one sitting you updated the network configuration and also started trying out some experimental feature flags, so both changes sit in the same file. terraform/debug.txt is in the folder too. Raven reviews the network change tomorrow, and she doesn't want to wonder what the flags are for.

Starting point: You are on main; local branches include main; working files include terraform/main.tf, terraform/debug.txt.
partial-hard-terraform.task: Stage only the network configuration hunk and commit it with the message Update network Terraform configuration. Leave The experimental flags and debug file out of the commit and finish on main.

partial-med-three-hunk.label: Stage only the parser bug fix hunk
partial-med-three-hunk.real_world_context: The parser file holds a finished bug fix, a refactor, and an experiment. Partial staging can save the fix alone while the other two sections stay available locally.
partial-med-three-hunk.story:
src/parser.py holds three separate pieces of work: a bug that made the importer choke on blank lines, which is fixed; a half-finished rewrite of token handling; and an experimental section you aren't sure about. Maeve will review the bug fix on its own.

Starting point: You are on main; local branches include main; working files include src/parser.py.
partial-med-three-hunk.task: Stage only the parser bug fix and commit it with the message Fix parser blank-line bug. Leave The refactor and experiment out of the commit and finish on main.

partial-medium-dashboard-filter.label: Stage only the dashboard filter hunk
partial-medium-dashboard-filter.real_world_context: The filter fix, theme work, and console output share a file but serve different purposes. Partial staging isolates the functional correction for review.
partial-medium-dashboard-filter.story:
src/dashboard.js has three changes: the filter logic you fixed, a theme update you were trying out, and some console.log lines left from debugging. notes/dashboard-ideas.md is still in the folder too. Finn needs the filter fix for tomorrow's demo, but the theme and the logging aren't something he should have to review.

Starting point: You are on main; local branches include main; working files include src/dashboard.js, notes/dashboard-ideas.md.
partial-medium-dashboard-filter.task: Stage only the dashboard filter fix and commit it with the message Fix dashboard filter. Leave The theme work, console output, and notes out of the commit and finish on main.

partial-medium-payment-rounding.label: Stage only the payment rounding hunk
partial-medium-payment-rounding.real_world_context: A payment rounding bug should be reviewed independently of logging and comments. Selecting its hunk also leaves the scratch file outside the saved change.
partial-medium-payment-rounding.story:
Over the afternoon you changed src/payment.py three ways: a rounding fix, some added logging, and a comment you reworded. tmp/payment-scratch.txt is also in your folder from your test calculations. Raven's rule is one reason per commit, so you're stopping before you save any of it. Only the rounding fix belongs to the bug report.

Starting point: You are on main; local branches include main; working files include src/payment.py, tmp/payment-scratch.txt.
partial-medium-payment-rounding.task: Stage only the payment rounding fix and commit it with the message Fix payment rounding. Leave The logging, comment edit, and scratch file out of the commit and finish on main.

partial-medium-profile-validation.label: Stage only the profile validation hunk
partial-medium-profile-validation.real_world_context: The validation change is ready, but copy and cleanup edits are still in progress. A focused patch keeps that unfinished work and the notes file out of the commit.
partial-medium-profile-validation.story:
src/profile.py has three changes in it: a validation fix, a wording update for the profile page, and a cleanup you haven't finished. Next to it, notes/profile-todo.md is still full of your reminders. Only the validation fix is ready for Sage to review.

Starting point: You are on main; local branches include main; working files include src/profile.py, notes/profile-todo.md.
partial-medium-profile-validation.task: Stage only the profile validation fix and commit it with the message Fix profile validation. Leave The copy, cleanup, and notes out of the commit and finish on main.

pull-med-free-client.label: Pull origin/staging into local staging
pull-med-free-client.real_world_context: The client’s staging edits must be present locally before you continue the preview work.
pull-med-free-client.story:
Your client has updated the preview content on origin/staging. You are on your own staging branch and need those changes before you keep building the preview. Sage says, “If we skip their update, our next screenshot will show yesterday’s copy.” The remote is already configured as origin. Pull its staging branch into your current local branch so your preview work starts from the client’s latest content.

Starting point: You are on staging; available local branches: staging; origin is available.
pull-med-free-client.task: Bring the latest origin/staging commits into your current local staging branch.

push-easy-cap-auth.label: Push feature/user-auth to origin
push-easy-cap-auth.real_world_context: Groupmates can fetch a pushed authentication branch to test it on their own machines.
push-easy-cap-auth.story:
Your capstone group’s authentication work is done on feature/user-auth. In the group chat, one classmate asks to test the sign-in screen and another asks whether the commits are available yet. Raven checks the shared repository: your branch is still only local. origin is already configured. Publish the branch so your groupmates can fetch it; this request does not require setting up upstream tracking.

Starting point: You are on feature/user-auth; available local branches: feature/user-auth, main; origin is available.
push-easy-cap-auth.task: Publish the committed local feature/user-auth to origin for teammates to access.

push-easy-free-landing.label: Push feature/client-landing to origin
push-easy-free-landing.real_world_context: The client needs a remote branch to inspect the landing page work before accepting it.
push-easy-free-landing.story:
The client wants to review the landing page before you continue polishing it. You have finished and committed the draft on feature/client-landing, but a screenshot would not let the client inspect the code. Sage says, “Put your branch in the client’s repository and I’ll send them the review link.” Their repository is configured as origin. Publish the branch there; no upstream setup is requested for this handoff.

Starting point: You are on feature/client-landing; available local branches: feature/client-landing, main; origin is available.
push-easy-free-landing.task: Publish the committed local feature/client-landing to origin for teammates to access.

push-hard-devops-fwl.label: Publish rewritten feature/pipeline-config without overwriting a teammate's work
push-hard-devops-fwl.real_world_context: After history is rewritten, an ordinary push is rejected because the remote still holds the old commits. A guarded forced update replaces the remote branch only if nobody has added to it since you last looked, so a teammate's newer work is never wiped out.
push-hard-devops-fwl.story:
The CI team asks you to remove debug commits from feature/pipeline-config before review. You clean the branch locally, and the new history looks tidy, but origin still has the older chain of commits and a normal push is rejected. Sage says, “I want the cleaner branch up there, but I also want to know if somebody touched the remote while we worked.”

Starting point: You are on feature/pipeline-config; available local branches: feature/pipeline-config, main; origin is available. Your local feature/pipeline-config history was rewritten; origin/feature/pipeline-config still has the older commits.
push-hard-devops-fwl.task: Update origin/feature/pipeline-config so it matches your rewritten local feature/pipeline-config. The update must be refused if the remote branch has commits you have not seen. Do not use an unconditional force.

push-med-docs-track.label: Push feature/v2-migration-guide and set its upstream
push-med-docs-track.real_world_context: The documentation branch will need more edits. Upstream tracking avoids typing its long name on each later push.
push-med-docs-track.story:
The migration guide for version 2 is nearly drafted, and the documentation team wants to start leaving comments today. feature/v2-migration-guide exists only on your laptop, and you'll be pushing updates to it all week. Raven would like your pushes and pulls to just work without typing out the full branch name every time.

Starting point: You are on feature/v2-migration-guide; available local branches: feature/v2-migration-guide, main; origin is available.
push-med-docs-track.task: Publish feature/v2-migration-guide to origin and set the corresponding remote branch as its upstream.

rb-easy-cap-group.label: Delete origin/feature/group-auth
rb-easy-cap-group.real_world_context: The group already merged authentication. Removing the remote feature branch prevents classmates from starting new work on a closed line.
rb-easy-cap-group.story:
Your capstone group merged feature/group-auth into main yesterday, then moved straight to presentation slides. Sage opens the remote branch list today and finds the old feature name still there. “Let’s leave a tidy repository for the next group member,” she says. You are on main, with the shared remote named origin. Delete feature/group-auth from that remote; your local branch can remain.

Starting point: You are on main; available local branches: main, feature/group-auth. origin is available and has the branch.
rb-easy-cap-group.task: Delete the merged feature/group-auth branch from origin. Keep the local branch.

rb-easy-corp-sprint.label: Delete origin/feature/sprint12-compliance
rb-easy-corp-sprint.real_world_context: The tracker says the sprint branch is closed, so its remote name no longer needs to appear among active branches.
rb-easy-corp-sprint.story:
Sprint 12 is closed in the project tracker, and the compliance feature has already been merged. Raven sees feature/sprint12-compliance still sitting on origin, making the branch list look as though the ticket is open. You are on main. “Remove the shared branch name so it matches the tracker,” she says. Delete that remote branch; this task does not ask you to remove your separate local copy.

Starting point: You are on main; available local branches: main, feature/sprint12-compliance. origin is available and has the branch.
rb-easy-corp-sprint.task: Delete the merged feature/sprint12-compliance branch from origin. Keep the local branch.

rb-hard-oss-full.label: Retire feature/oss-contribution on origin and locally
rb-hard-oss-full.real_world_context: The contribution is integrated. Cleaning up both branch names leaves the repository focused on active work.
rb-hard-oss-full.story:
The open source maintainer merges your contribution and thanks you for the fix. Raven checks your fork afterward: feature/oss-contribution still exists on its origin remote and in your local repository. The pull request is done, and you are back on main. “Let’s close the loop,” she says. Your contribution remains in the project’s merged history.

Starting point: You are on main; available local branches: main, feature/oss-contribution. origin is available and has the branch.
rb-hard-oss-full.task: The feature/oss-contribution branch has been merged, so retire it everywhere: remove it from origin and remove your local copy, but only through a route that would refuse to delete unmerged work. Finish on main.

rb-med-free-prune.label: Prune stale origin/feature/old-landing ref
rb-med-free-prune.real_world_context: The client removed the old landing branch remotely; pruning removes the obsolete local record of it while leaving local branches alone.
rb-med-free-prune.story:
The client abandoned an old landing page concept and deleted feature/old-landing from their remote repository. Sage checks your branch list and still sees origin/feature/old-landing because your local view has not been refreshed. You are on main, and your separate local feature branch remains. “Let’s show what is actually on the server,” she says. Fetch from origin with pruning to clear the stale remote tracking name; keep the local branch.

Starting point: You are on main; available local branches: main, feature/old-landing; origin is available.
rb-med-free-prune.task: Refresh remote tracking information from origin and remove the stale origin/feature/old-landing record. Keep your local feature/old-landing branch.

re6.label: Revert c3 safely
re6.real_world_context: Revert adds a new commit that reverses an earlier change. Teammates can receive it by an ordinary push without rewriting shared history.
re6.story:
QA catches a risky configuration change only after it has reached the shared main branch. Finn checks the history and identifies the published change as c3. Other teammates may already have pulled the branch, so he wants a new correction recorded in history and sent to origin. “Let’s undo that one change without making their histories jump backward,” he says. You are on local main. Reverse c3 with a new commit and publish the updated branch.

Starting point: You are on main; available local branches: main; origin is available and main tracks origin/main.
re6.task: Create a new commit on main that reverses c3, then push the correction to origin.

re7.label: Revert c2 safely
re7.real_world_context: A published branch should keep its history stable for collaborators. Reverting the banner change produces a new correction they can pull.
re7.story:
The marketing agency’s homepage looks fine on a laptop but collapses on a phone after a promo banner goes live. Sage traces the banner to published commit c2. The rest of the team is already working from main, so she asks for a new rollback commit that everyone can receive normally. You are on local main, with origin available. Reverse the effect of c2, then publish the correction so the mobile layout is usable again.

Starting point: You are on main; available local branches: main; origin is available and main tracks origin/main.
re7.task: Create a new commit on main that reverses c2, then push the correction to origin.

re8.label: Revert c4 safely
re8.real_world_context: A targeted revert backs out the faulty timeout setting while leaving other published commits in place.
re8.story:
The payment API begins timing out on ordinary slow requests right after a new setting is published. Raven compares the history and points to commit c4. “We need that setting undone, but we still need the later work in the shared branch,” she says. You are on main, and the team remote is available. Create a new commit that reverses c4, then push the corrected history so other developers can pick it up.

Starting point: You are on main; available local branches: main; origin is available and main tracks origin/main.
re8.task: Create a new commit on main that reverses c4, then push the correction to origin.

rec-easy-cap-ui.label: Reconcile and push feature/ui-layout
rec-easy-cap-ui.real_world_context: The files do not overlap, so this exercise expects the pull to integrate cleanly before you push the combined UI branch.
rec-easy-cap-ui.story:
Your groupmate changes the UI layout while you are changing a different file on the same feature branch. When you try to push feature/ui-layout, Git refuses because the groupmate’s commit arrived first. Sage checks the files: the changes do not overlap, so this exercise should integrate cleanly. You are already on the local feature branch. Pull the remote version into it, then push again so both contributions are available to the group.

Starting point: You are on feature/ui-layout; available local branches: feature/ui-layout; origin is available.
rec-easy-cap-ui.task: Pull origin/feature/ui-layout into your current local branch to reconcile the rejected push, then push feature/ui-layout again.

rec-easy-docs-chapter.label: Reconcile and push main
rec-easy-docs-chapter.real_world_context: Both documentation commits belong on main. Bring the colleague’s chapter in before sharing your own update.
rec-easy-docs-chapter.story:
You and a colleague are writing separate chapters in the documentation repository. Your push to main fails because your colleague published a chapter while yours was still local. Raven compares the changes and sees that the files do not overlap. “We need both chapters,” she says. You are on local main, with origin configured. Pull the new remote commit into your branch, then push the combined documentation back to the shared repository.

Starting point: You are on main; available local branches: main; origin is available.
rec-easy-docs-chapter.task: Pull origin/main into your current local branch to reconcile the rejected push, then push main again.

rec-hard-corp-audit.label: Reconcile and publish the audit branch from develop
rec-hard-corp-audit.real_world_context: An audit branch should be reconciled on that branch, not on develop, so the resulting push updates the intended review work.
rec-hard-corp-audit.story:
Sage needs the compliance audit work published for review. Your earlier push to feature/compliance-audit was rejected because another teammate updated that branch first. You are currently on develop, which should not receive any of the audit work. The local audit branch already exists.

Starting point: You are on develop; available local branches: develop, feature/compliance-audit; origin is available.
rec-hard-corp-audit.task: Combine the teammate's newer origin/feature/compliance-audit work with your own commits on feature/compliance-audit, and publish the combined result to origin. develop must not receive any of this work. Finish on feature/compliance-audit.

rec-med-qa-testrunner.label: Fetch, merge, push feature/test-runner-v2
rec-med-qa-testrunner.real_world_context: The test runner branch is shared by QA teammates. An explicit fetch and merge preserves their published fixes alongside yours.
rec-med-qa-testrunner.story:
The QA team is preparing a new test runner, and Sage notices your push to feature/test-runner-v2 has been rejected. Another tester added fixes to the same remote branch. “Let’s see their commit before we combine it with yours,” she says. You are on the local feature branch. Fetch from origin, explicitly merge its updated test runner branch, and then push the combined work for the rest of QA to use.

Starting point: You are on feature/test-runner-v2; available local branches: feature/test-runner-v2; origin is available.
rec-med-qa-testrunner.task: Fetch from origin, merge origin/feature/test-runner-v2 into your current feature/test-runner-v2 branch, then push the combined result.

restore-easy-discard.label: Discard experimental config.py changes
restore-easy-discard.real_world_context: An unsuccessful configuration experiment can be replaced with the last committed version. Restoring this tracked file clears the unwanted local edit.
restore-easy-discard.story:
You spent an hour trying a new approach in config.py, and it didn't work. The edits are still in your folder. You want the file back exactly as the last commit left it, and nothing in these edits is worth keeping.

Starting point: You are on main; local branches include main; working files include config.py.
restore-easy-discard.task: Discard the working-tree changes in config.py and restore the committed version. Finish on main.

restore-easy-unstage.label: Unstage notes.txt without discarding it
restore-easy-unstage.real_world_context: Staging notes.txt does not mean its edits are lost when it is removed from the index. Unstaging keeps the notes available for a later commit.
restore-easy-unstage.story:
You staged everything with one quick command and notes.txt came along with the files you meant to commit. The notes are yours, not the project's, and you still want them. The commit isn't ready.

Starting point: You are on main; local branches include main; some changes are staged.
restore-easy-unstage.task: Unstage notes.txt while keeping those edits. Finish on main.

restore-easy-unstage-app.label: Unstage src/app.py without discarding it
restore-easy-unstage-app.real_world_context: The app change still needs work, so it should wait outside the next commit. Unstaging keeps the edited source file in the working tree.
restore-easy-unstage-app.story:
You staged src/app.py and then realized it isn't ready. There's still a function you haven't finished, and the commit would have broken the build for Sage. Your edits to the file should survive.

Starting point: You are on main; local branches include main; some changes are staged.
restore-easy-unstage-app.task: Unstage src/app.py while keeping those edits. Finish on main.

restore-easy-unstage-css.label: Unstage styles/site.css without discarding it
restore-easy-unstage-css.real_world_context: The CSS change will be committed with another styling update later. Unstaging keeps the current edit while the developer prepares the complete set.
restore-easy-unstage-css.story:
You staged styles/site.css and then realized another CSS change belongs in the same commit. If you commit now, the change is split in two. Your edits to the file must stay, and you'll group everything later.

Starting point: You are on main; local branches include main; some changes are staged.
restore-easy-unstage-css.task: Unstage styles/site.css while keeping those edits. Finish on main.

restore-easy-unstage-guide.label: Unstage docs/guide.md without discarding it
restore-easy-unstage-guide.real_world_context: A guide that needs another revision should not be part of the next snapshot yet. Unstaging preserves its current edits for continued writing.
restore-easy-unstage-guide.story:
You staged docs/guide.md, then decided to revise it more before it goes into a commit. The edits you've made so far are good work and need to stay in your folder.

Starting point: You are on main; local branches include main; some changes are staged.
restore-easy-unstage-guide.task: Unstage docs/guide.md while keeping those edits. Finish on main.

restore-hard-cleanup.label: Unstage two files, discard experimental.py
restore-hard-cleanup.real_world_context: A mixed workspace may contain staged notes worth keeping and an experiment worth abandoning. Removing files from staging does not discard their edits; restoring the experiment does.
restore-hard-cleanup.story:
Your folder is in a messy mixed state. debug.log and scratch/notes.txt are staged, though neither belongs in the next commit, and you still want both. api/experimental.py has edits you've decided are a dead end. Nothing is going to be committed tonight, and once the dead-end edits are discarded they're gone for good.

Starting point: You are on main; local branches include main; working files include api/experimental.py; some changes are staged.
restore-hard-cleanup.task: Unstage debug.log, scratch/notes.txt while keeping those edits. Discard the working-tree changes in api/experimental.py and restore their committed versions. Finish on main.

restore-hard-mixed-export.label: Unstage two files, discard generated output
restore-hard-mixed-export.real_world_context: The export code and plan should remain editable after they leave staging. The tracked generated output can return to its committed state.
restore-hard-mixed-export.story:
src/export.py and notes/export-plan.md are staged, though you intend to keep working on both before committing. tmp/export-output.txt is generated output that keeps changing every time you run a test. Raven wants tonight's folder clean, but nothing needs to be committed, and what gets thrown away can't come back.

Starting point: You are on main; local branches include main; working files include tmp/export-output.txt; some changes are staged.
